newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Young New Zealanders swell Anzac remembrance crowds.
newsitem.headline: Young New Zealanders swell Anzac remembrance crowds.

text.p: Hundreds of young people swelled crowds at traditional remembrance services across New Zealand on Friday on the anniversary of the World War One landings of troops from Australasia on Gallipoli in Turkey.
Crowds several thousand strong attended dawn services and watched veterans of several wars march in the main cities on the country's North and South Islands.

Anzac day, the anniversary of the landing of the Australian and New Zealand Army Corps (ANZAC) on April 25, 1915, on a Gallipoli beachhead, is deeply significant to the two countries because of the heavy loss of life in the campaign.
Both contributed large numbers of soldiers to the campaign and few families escaped the suffering of losing a loved one.
Only one Gallipoli veteran, 100-year-old Doug Dibley, survives in New Zealand with another 10 in Australia.
Veterans' association representatives told national radio on Friday they believed crowds had grown again this year, continuing a recent trend of more young people joining events.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger, in an address to the National War Memorial service in Wellington, said New Zealanders should use the courageous spirit shown in a century of modern wars to confront the troubled legacy of the country's past.
Both Bolger and other political leaders said the day drew attention to the lack of cohesion found in modern New Zealand and Australia as they struggled with questions of nationhood.

Bolger highlighted current disputes in New Zealand over rights and reparations as a government-established tribunal considers breaches of the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi between Maori and European settlers.

"In our case, not only the sense of nationhood forged in the fires of adversity in distant battles, but also the sense of nationhood that began at the peaceful village of Waitangi 157 years ago (is at issue)," he said.
